headline: S&P Global moves to buy data center site-selection data firm datacenterHawk
players: S&P Global has agreed to acquire datacenterHawk, a firm founded in 2014 that tracks hundreds of data center markets, covering operating facilities, projects under development, pricing, available capacity and fiber connectivity. Terms were not disclosed in the reporting.
why_it_matters: As hyperscalers and infrastructure funds race to site gigawatt-scale campuses, proprietary data on power availability and grid capacity is becoming as valuable as the real estate itself. A ratings/data giant buying into that layer signals underwriting for data center and power deals is getting more data-driven and less bespoke, which could compress the information edge sponsors like DigitalBridge or GIP have relied on.
why_you_care: Useful context for any pitch or comp involving data center power siting — the tools underwriters use to value sites are consolidating.

headline: Appeals court upholds FERC's 2023 interconnection queue reform rule against industry challenges
players: The DC Circuit Court of Appeals sided with FERC on Friday, upholding the 2023 order that added study deadlines and penalties to how transmission providers process interconnection requests. The rule was challenged by industry parties as exceeding FERC's authority; the court disagreed.
why_it_matters: This is the rulebook that governs how fast a wind, solar, storage or gas project can get through the interconnection queue and start earning revenue. Upholding it removes a legal cloud over queue reform just as FERC is separately pushing grid operators to speed up large-load and data center interconnections. Watch for how PJM, MISO and others cite this ruling in their pending Section 206 responses.
why_you_care: Queue speed directly affects when a renewables asset like an ArcLight/Avangrid wind or solar project starts generating cash flow.

headline: Blackstone Energy Transition Partners to acquire industrial imaging firm DarkVision from Koch
players: Blackstone Energy Transition Partners agreed to acquire DarkVision from Koch Engineered Solutions; terms undisclosed. Founded in 2013 and headquartered in North Vancouver, DarkVision employs roughly 300 people and builds ultrasound imaging technology that converts sensor data into photorealistic 3D visuals for assessing integrity and defects in critical industrial and energy infrastructure. Its stack spans imaging sensors and silicon through defect-quantifying AI models and rendering software; close is subject to customary conditions.
why_it_matters: Asset integrity inspection is regulatory-driven, non-discretionary spend across pipelines, wells and industrial plant, so revenue recurs and is largely insulated from commodity price swings. Owning the whole stack, from imaging sensors and silicon through defect-quantifying AI models, is a real moat in a market where competitors resell hardware and interpret data manually. Coming a month after Dresser, it confirms Blackstone's energy transition vehicle is pivoting from asset ownership to services. Terms undisclosed.
why_you_care: A competing sponsor answering high infrastructure entry multiples by buying energy services rather than assets, on regulatory-driven inspection spend. Second such deal in a month.

headline: INNIO wins a 1.1-GW gas engine order from a US data center developer covering 200+ Jenbacher J624 units
players: INNIO announced on July 30, 2026 an order of approximately 1.1 GW of gas engine capacity from an unnamed developer and operator of large-scale US data center campuses, comprising more than 200 Jenbacher J624 engines on a phased delivery schedule. INNIO cited containerized, fast-deployment configurations as the basis for the award; the customer was not disclosed for confidentiality reasons.
why_it_matters: INNIO announced an order of roughly 1.1 GW of gas engine capacity from an unnamed US data center campus developer, more than 200 Jenbacher J624 units on a phased schedule, won on containerised fast-deployment configurations. Developers have stopped waiting for large gas turbines and are buying deliverable capacity, which shifts value to engine OEMs and balance-of-plant contractors. It also means behind-the-meter capacity at higher heat rates than combined cycle.
why_you_care: Hard evidence for the behind-the-meter gas thesis: developers buying deliverable engines instead of waiting on turbines, which scales the aftermarket demand pool behind names like Sisu and Miratech.

headline: Commonwealth Fusion raises $1B, taking total to $4B, with a 400-MW ARC plant in Virginia and a 200-MW Google PPA
players: Commonwealth Fusion Systems raised $1 billion in equity financing announced July 30, 2026, bringing total capital raised to $4 billion — the most of any fusion company — following a $1.8 billion Series B in 2021 and an $863 million Series B2 in 2025. Its commercial ARC plant, planned at 400 MW at the James River Industrial Park in Chesterfield County, Virginia in partnership with Dominion Energy, is expected to deliver electricity to the grid in the early 2030s, with Google committed to purchasing 200 MW on completion. The SPARC demonstration machine targets first plasma in 2027.
why_it_matters: CFS raised another $1bn, taking it to $4bn total, but the notable term is Google committing to buy 200MW from a pre-commercial technology: hyperscalers will write long-dated offtake against unproven generation to lock in 2030s clean-firm capacity. Siting the 400MW ARC plant in Dominion's power-constrained Virginia territory is deliberate. Fusion stays uninvestable as infrastructure until SPARC demonstrates net energy; first plasma is targeted for 2027.
why_you_care: Not investable as infrastructure until SPARC shows net energy, but Google committing to buy 200MW on completion is the clearest read on how hyperscaler offtake reprices clean firm power.

headline: Lightpath says IP backbone traffic is growing 32% annualised as AI workloads scale across its 12,100-mile network
players: Lightpath, the US metro fibre platform jointly owned by Optimum Communications (NYSE: OPTU) and MSIP, disclosed that IP traffic across its network has grown at a 32% annualised rate over the most recent 18 months, against a 19% historical annual rate. The network now spans 12,100 route miles across 11 major US metro markets with more than 18,000 connected service locations. No financial figures disclosed.
why_it_matters: IP traffic across Lightpath's 12,100 route miles has grown at a 32% annualised rate over 18 months, against a 19% historical rate. Traffic leads recontracting and upsell, because bandwidth upgrades on already-lit buildings drop through at very high margin with the capex sunk. The step-change suggests Lightpath is capturing AI-era traffic, not just legacy enterprise access, supporting terminal value on an asset MSIP has held since 2020.
why_you_care: MSIP portfolio company: 32% annualised IP traffic growth against 19% historically, upsell on already-lit buildings at very high margin, supporting terminal value on an asset held since 2020.

headline: FirstEnergy's contracted data center load jumps 50% in one quarter to 6.4 GW; total pipeline reaches 24.8 GW
players: FirstEnergy reported on July 30, 2026 that contracted data center load reached 6.4 GW in Q2, a 50% increase from Q1, with another 1.5 GW of contracts expected within two weeks and a total pipeline including prospective customers of 24.8 GW, up 30% in the quarter. West Virginia alone accounts for a 4.1 GW pipeline, up 155% from 1.6 GW in Q1. FirstEnergy subsidiaries Monongahela Power and Potomac Edison are seeking West Virginia PSC approval for the Maidsville Energy Center — a 1,200-MW gas plant estimated at $2.5 billion plus three solar projects totaling 70 MW at $182 million — targeted for end-2031 operation, with an approximately 2.3% residential rate increase; opponents note the associated data center's ramp has already slipped two years.
why_it_matters: FirstEnergy reported 6.4 GW of contracted data centre load in Q2, up 50% from Q1, with 1.5 GW more expected within two weeks and a 24.8 GW total pipeline, up 30%; West Virginia alone is 4.1 GW, up 155%. Its utilities are seeking WV PSC approval for the 1,200-MW, $2.5bn Maidsville gas plant plus 70 MW of solar at $182m, in service end-2031, with a 2.3% residential rate rise. The associated data centre has already slipped two years.
why_you_care: Who pays if the load arrives late: a $2.5bn, 1,200-MW gas plant and a 2.3% residential rate rise against a data centre that has already slipped two years.

headline: Entergy's $1.8B purchase of the 1.26-GW Cottonwood gas plant for Meta-driven load runs into Louisiana regulatory resistance
players: Entergy's proposed $1.8 billion acquisition of the 1.26-GW Cottonwood plant in Texas from Atlas Holdings, intended to serve Meta data centers in Entergy's service territory, faces Louisiana Public Service Commission staff analysis finding it could add upwards of $7 per month to bills for a customer using 1,000 kWh. Entergy says Meta will pay grid maintenance and upgrade costs, potentially saving residential and small business customers more than $2.65 billion over two decades. CEO Drew Marsh acknowledged 'Cottonwood isn't the shiniest new plant out there' and the utility is seeking additional industrial customers including steel mills, LNG facilities and petrochemical operations to spread costs; analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith called the deal 'increasingly in doubt.' Entergy hopes to close by Q1 2027.
why_it_matters: Entergy's proposed $1.8bn purchase of the 1.26-GW Cottonwood plant from Atlas Holdings, to serve Meta data centers, is the first big test of whether regulators will let a utility rate-base an existing merchant gas plant for one hyperscaler. At $1.43m per MW it is the comparable for aging Gulf CCGT. LPSC staff put the bill impact at up to $7 a month; one analyst calls the deal 'increasingly in doubt.'
why_you_care: Sets the gas-to-power comp for aging Gulf CCGT at $1.43m per MW, and the LPSC outcome decides whether merchant gas owners get a utility exit channel at all.

headline: Shell CEO says LNG Canada Phase 2 final investment decision is likely by the end of 2026
players: Shell chief executive Wael Sawan confirmed on July 30, 2026 that Shell and its LNG Canada partners expect to take a final investment decision on Phase 2 of the Kitimat project by the end of the year. The statement follows the limited notice to proceed issued to the JGC Fluor BC LNG II joint venture in June for early engineering and procurement.
why_it_matters: Shell CEO Wael Sawan said Shell and its LNG Canada partners expect a final investment decision on Phase 2 at Kitimat by year-end, following June's limited notice to proceed to the JGC Fluor BC LNG II joint venture. That moves Phase 2 from an option to a base case for Western Canadian gas balances and Coastal GasLink throughput, while tightening competition for BC coast labour and long-lead equipment.
why_you_care: Background midstream colour for now, but the capex disclosed at FID would set the cost-per-tonne benchmark for Canadian LNG against US Gulf supply.

headline: Aalo and Crusoe plan a 2027 nuclear-powered AI data center demo at INL, scaling to 50-MWe reactor plants by 2029
players: Aalo Atomics and Crusoe announced a partnership under which Aalo will power a Crusoe Spark modular data center running Crusoe Cloud at Idaho National Laboratory in 2027 as a proof of concept, followed by deployment of Aalo Pods and 50-MWe extra-modular reactor plants at Crusoe data centers by end of 2029. The Aalo Pod is a 50-MW system comprising five 10-MWe Aalo-1 reactors sharing a turbine. The announcement follows Aalo's Critical Test Reactor achieving criticality at INL on July 4, 2026, the fourth DOE-authorized advanced reactor milestone that month.
why_it_matters: A 2029 target for commercial nuclear-powered data centre capacity is well ahead of the early-2030s consensus, and if it holds it pulls forward the point at which nuclear competes with gas on speed-to-power. The pod design, five 10-MWe reactors sharing one turbine, trades unit size for factory replication. Still venture-stage risk, but criticality at INL and a named compute offtaker help.
why_you_care: A 2029 target for commercial nuclear-powered data centre capacity sits well ahead of the early-2030s consensus; still venture-stage risk, but a concrete timeline for nuclear competing with gas on speed.

headline: Texas regulators approve Crusoe's 260-MW data center co-located with a wind farm, but require full curtailment in 30 minutes
players: The Public Utility Commission of Texas approved a net metering arrangement on July 24, 2026 for a 260-MW Crusoe data center co-located with roughly 265.5 MW of wind generation, with Ensign as the large load customer. The data center must curtail its full load within 30 minutes during grid emergencies, with physical breaker disconnection if necessary; ERCOT is to give 60 minutes' notice 'when practicable,' and the operator may voluntarily commit to a 10-minute response. The project cannot participate in paid demand response tied to the arrangement, and the condition applies to an earlier co-located load as well, despite combined capacity of 525 MW exceeding the 265.5 MW of generation. Analysts said the framework essentially requires full backup capacity and may serve as the template for a pending Amazon-Vistra proposal near Comanche Peak.
why_it_matters: Texas approved net metering for a 260-MW Crusoe data center co-located with roughly 265.5 MW of wind, but the load must curtail fully within 30 minutes in a grid emergency, with physical breaker disconnection if needed, and cannot take paid demand response. That effectively obliges full backup capacity, changing the capex stack for every co-location pro forma and capping the arbitrage value of sitting behind intermittent generation.
why_you_care: Changes the co-location pro forma: a 30-minute full-curtailment obligation with no paid demand response forces full backup capex and caps the arbitrage value of sitting behind intermittent generation.

headline: DOE reconsiders the 2024 distribution transformer efficiency rule, splitting utilities and Cleveland-Cliffs
players: Utility Dive reported on July 29, 2026 that DOE is weighing revisions to 2024 distribution transformer efficiency standards, having requested public comment in June 2026 on effects including domestic manufacturing capacity, supply chain resilience and materials cost. The 2024 rule takes effect in April 2029 and requires greater use of amorphous electrical steel alongside grain-oriented electrical steel. Most utilities oppose repeal — Edison Electric Institute asked instead for extended compliance timelines, saying flexibility preserves efficiency gains while giving the electrical steel supply chain more time. Cleveland-Cliffs, the sole North American GOES producer, reversed its earlier support and asked DOE to retain the 2016 standards indefinitely or adopt different benchmarks. Transformer lead times currently exceed 18 months.
why_it_matters: DOE is weighing revisions to the 2024 distribution transformer efficiency standards, which take effect April 2029 and require more amorphous electrical steel; it sought comment in June on manufacturing capacity, supply chain resilience and materials cost. Most utilities oppose repeal, with EEI asking instead for longer compliance timelines, while Cleveland-Cliffs, the only North American GOES producer, reversed course and wants the 2016 standards kept. Lead times already exceed 18 months.
why_you_care: Transformers gate every energisation schedule in data centre power, and lead times already exceed 18 months, so the rule revision is the supply-chain variable behind your build timelines.

headline: McDermott and ULC-Energy sign cooperation agreement to advance Rolls-Royce SMR projects in the Netherlands and Belgium
players: McDermott and Amsterdam-based nuclear developer ULC-Energy signed a cooperation agreement to support Rolls-Royce SMR projects, focused on integrating SMR-powered energy solutions with energy-intensive industrial processes in the Netherlands and Belgium. McDermott will contribute engineering expertise across energy transition, industrial decarbonisation, low-carbon hydrogen and ammonia, sustainable aviation fuel and carbon capture. The companies previously collaborated on a 2023 study. No contract value or timeline was disclosed and the binding nature of the agreement was not specified; McDermott joins a partner network including Siemens Energy, BAM, Mammoet, Bureau Veritas, Urenco, Orano and Fugro.
why_it_matters: McDermott and Amsterdam-based ULC-Energy signed a cooperation agreement to support Rolls-Royce SMR projects, aimed at pairing SMRs with energy-intensive industry in the Netherlands and Belgium, with McDermott supplying engineering across decarbonisation, hydrogen, ammonia, SAF and carbon capture. No contract value, timeline or binding status was disclosed, so nothing belongs in backlog. It lands four weeks after the Nordic bond pricing and during the rights offering subscription period.
why_you_care: You ran McDermott/NMDC at Rothschild. Positioning rather than an award, with no value, timeline or binding status disclosed, but it lands during the rights offering subscription period.

headline: Ratepayer Protection Pledge reaches 281 entities and 23 states covering about 80% of US power delivery
players: The Ratepayer Protection Pledge, convened by the Trump administration, commits signatories not to shift data center costs to electricity customers in the form of higher bills. Initial technology signatories include Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon; utility signatories include Ameren, American Electric Power, Arizona Public Service, Dominion Energy, DTE Energy, Duke Energy, Entergy, Nebraska Public Power District, NextEra Energy, PG&E Corporation, PSEG, Southern Company, TVA and Xcel Energy. As of July 29, 2026, 281 entities and 23 states had signed on, covering approximately 80% of US power delivery.
why_it_matters: A voluntary pledge covering roughly 80% of US power delivery, 281 entities and 23 states, becomes the de facto standard regulators apply in every large-load rate case whether or not it has legal force. In practice data centre customers fund their own generation, transmission and distribution through tariffs, collateral and take-or-pay: good for utility credit and rate base growth, expensive for hyperscalers and colocation providers. That pushes them toward behind-the-meter self-supply.
why_you_care: Underwriting input for anything data-centre adjacent: if large loads fund their own generation and network through tariffs and take-or-pay, grid power stops being the cheap option.

headline: July 4 safe-harbour deadline passes for US renewable tax credits without derailing the solar and wind outlook
players: Infrastructure Investor reported on July 29, 2026 that July 4, 2026 marked the closure of the safe-harbour period for renewable tax credits once deemed vital to the sector, and that the sunsetting of those credits does not dim the outlook for US solar and wind. The deadline followed the June 6, 2026 court decision restoring the 5% cost safe harbor for beginning of construction.
why_it_matters: Infrastructure Investor reported that the July 4 safe-harbour window for renewable tax credits has closed and argued the sunset does not dim the US solar and wind outlook. In practice, eligibility is now a fixed attribute of each project, making safe-harboured pipelines and their equipment inventories scarcer and more valuable. It also pushes the marginal investment case toward merchant and corporate PPA economics rather than tax equity.
why_you_care: Eligibility is now a fixed attribute of each project, so safe-harboured pipelines get scarcer and dearer while the rest clears on merchant economics. Widens the bid-ask on any pipeline you mark.

headline: Antin sells 30% of Norwegian wellboat operator Sølvtrans to GLIL Infrastructure
players: Antin Infrastructure Partners' Flagship Fund III agreed to sell a 30% stake in Sølvtrans to UK investment fund GLIL Infrastructure, with Antin retaining majority ownership alongside founder Roger Halsebakk and his family; terms undisclosed. Ålesund-headquartered Sølvtrans is the largest provider of wellboats to the aquaculture industry, operating 48 vessels with eight more under construction, up from 21 vessels when Antin invested in 2018. Close is expected in Q3 2026 after an eight-year hold.
why_it_matters: Antin's Fund III agreed to sell 30% of Sølvtrans to GLIL Infrastructure, keeping majority control alongside the founder; terms undisclosed, close expected Q3 2026 after an eight-year hold. It generates DPI without a full exit at an uncertain point in the salmon cycle. Wellboats are contracted, mission-critical assets, the fleet grew from 21 vessels in 2018 to 48 with eight building, and GLIL's UK base targets Scottish expansion.
why_you_care: Partial stake sale as the DPI answer when holds stretch to eight years: Antin keeps control and the founder stays, with close expected in Q3 2026 and terms undisclosed.

headline: Bain Capital explores selling up to 50% of Singapore's Bridge DC at a roughly $4B valuation
players: Bain Capital is reported to be exploring a sale of up to a 50% stake in Singapore-based Bridge Data Centres at approximately a $4 billion valuation, with Sixth Street Partners, SK Telecom, GIC and La Caisse among the bidders. Bridge has five data centers operational or planned in Malaysia, two in Thailand and one in India, and targets 3 GW of capacity by 2030. Founded in 2017, Bridge was merged with Bain's ChinData business in 2019 and separated after ChinData's sale in September 2025. Bridge declined to comment on what it called unverified market information; no final decisions have been made.
why_it_matters: Bain is reported to be exploring a sale of up to 50% of Bridge Data Centres at roughly $4bn, with Sixth Street, SK Telecom, GIC and La Caisse among bidders; nothing has been decided. That is a useful pricing reference for emerging-market data centre growth capital, valued on pipeline (Bridge targets 3GW by 2030) rather than stabilised NOI, and it confirms Malaysia and Thailand as Singapore's overflow markets.
why_you_care: Pricing reference for emerging-market data centre platforms, valued on a 3GW pipeline rather than stabilised NOI; the bidder list shows which capital pools now compete. Nothing decided.

headline: CMS Energy to sell ~1.8 GW of non-utility renewables for about $500M net to concentrate on regulated returns
players: CMS Energy announced on July 29, 2026 plans to sell the non-utility renewable energy development operations of its NorthStar Clean Energy Services subsidiary — approximately 1.8 GW of generation across Michigan, Ohio, Texas and other states — for roughly $500 million in net proceeds. CMS will retain Michigan-based assets including a 770-MW cogeneration plant, two gas-fired peakers and about 500 MW of solar. CFO Srikanth Maddipati said the company is 'reallocating capital away from NorthStar so more of the upside and more of the growth will come from the utility,' targeting nearly all earnings from regulated utilities after 2027.
why_it_matters: CMS is selling NorthStar's non-utility renewables, roughly 1.8 GW across Michigan, Ohio, Texas and elsewhere, for about $500m net, aiming for nearly all earnings from regulated utilities after 2027. A utility choosing rate base over contracted renewables inverts the last decade's consensus, and it puts quality operating assets in front of infrastructure funds just as strategic buyers rotate out.
why_you_care: A utility putting roughly 1.8 GW of operating renewables in front of infrastructure funds at about $500m net. Live process, and your mark for operating US wind and solar.

headline: CPKC Q2 revenue up 13% to $4.2bn but operating ratio deteriorates 90 basis points to 64.6%
players: CPKC reported second quarter 2026 revenue of $4.2 billion, up 13% from $3.7 billion, with revenue ton-miles up 4%. Reported diluted EPS fell 14% to $1.15 while core adjusted diluted EPS rose 13% to $1.27. Operating ratio worsened 90 basis points to 64.6% and core adjusted OR worsened 90 basis points to 61.6%. CEO Keith Creel pointed to disciplined precision scheduled railroading execution and positioned the three-nation network for accelerated growth in the second half of 2026.
why_it_matters: Revenue up 13% on ton-miles up only 4% means price and mix carried the quarter, yet the operating ratio still slipped 90 basis points to 64.6%, so cost inflation is outrunning the pricing gain. That is a warning for anyone modelling more margin expansion in North American rail. As the only single-line US-Mexico-Canada carrier, CPKC's 4% RTM growth says nearshoring is real but gradual.
why_you_care: Live margin comp for rail models. Revenue up 13% on ton-miles up only 4% while the operating ratio still slipped 90 basis points means cost inflation is outrunning pricing gains.

headline: Georgia Ports June container volume up 18% to 483,684 TEU; FY26 closes at 5.67 million TEU
players: Georgia Ports Authority moved 483,684 TEU in June 2026, up 18% year on year, closing fiscal 2026 at 5.67 million TEU versus 5.7 million in FY25. The Mason Mega Rail facility handled 541,405 containers in FY26, a third consecutive year above half a million, with rail accounting for 17% of Savannah's container trade. The Appalachian Regional Port set a record 49,319 intermodal containers, up at least 20%. The Port of Brunswick moved 763,122 roll-on/roll-off units in FY26, down 12.4%, with June RoRo also down 12.4% at 58,599 units.
why_it_matters: Georgia Ports moved 483,684 TEU in June, up 18% year on year, closing FY26 at 5.67m TEU against 5.7m in FY25. Mason Mega Rail handled 541,405 containers, a third straight year above half a million, with rail at 17% of Savannah's container trade, and the Appalachian Regional Port set a record 49,319 intermodal containers. Brunswick RoRo fell 12.4% to 763,122 units.
why_you_care: Rail at 17% of Savannah's container trade is the inland-port datapoint worth keeping; Brunswick RoRo down 12.4% is the asymmetry when underwriting auto terminals against tariff risk.

headline: Brookfield and NextEra to build $100bn AI data centre campus at DOE's Paducah site with 4.6GW of dedicated generation
players: Brookfield and NextEra Energy will develop a privately funded $100bn AI data centre campus at the Department of Energy's Paducah site in western Kentucky, selected from a DOE Request for Offers issued in November 2025. Brookfield develops and operates the data centre on long-term DOE land leases; NextEra owns and operates up to 4.6GW of dedicated generation comprising up to 2GW of natural gas and up to 2.6GW of battery storage, added in stages. Big Rivers Electric provides wholesale service and Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative retail delivery; full buildout targets 2032 supporting up to 1.8GW of utility capacity and over 1.2GW of compute load, subject to Kentucky Public Service Commission approval.
why_it_matters: DOE awarded Brookfield a lease to develop a data centre campus at the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant in Kentucky and selected NextEra for power: up to 1.8 GW of utility capacity, over 1.2 GW of compute and 4.6 GW of dedicated generation, split 2 GW gas and 2.6 GW storage, fully built by 2032 at a reported $100bn. No offtaker disclosed, so it is a commitment to build, not a contract.
why_you_care: The largest live behind-the-fence gas-plus-storage structure on federal land, 4.6GW dedicated to one campus. No offtaker disclosed, so it is a commitment to build, not a contract.

headline: Western state lawmakers prepare a 2027 legislative wave targeting AI data centers and their power infrastructure
players: RTO Insider reported on July 28, 2026 that a potential wave of state legislation cracking down on the critical infrastructure needed to power the AI industry is shaping up as the defining Big Tech story of 2027, across western states including California, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah, Washington and Wyoming. The first half of 2026 was marked by the rise of opposition to and concerns about the impacts of hyperscale facilities.
why_it_matters: Siting and permitting risk is migrating from federal to state and local level, and western states with strong environmental review regimes can impose delays that federal permitting reform cannot cure. That raises the value of already-permitted, already-powered sites and widens the discount on greenfield land banks in contested jurisdictions. It also makes state-mandated cost allocation, water restrictions and clean-supply requirements more likely, lifting data centre operating costs.
why_you_care: Siting risk migrating to state level raises the value of already-permitted, already-powered sites and widens the discount on greenfield land banks, a direct input to how you price data centre land.

headline: ISO-NE picks $2.2bn Avangrid-Eversource solution in its first Longer-term Transmission Planning procurement
players: ISO New England on July 28, 2026 selected a $2.2 billion project from Avangrid and Eversource Energy as its preliminary preferred solution to Maine transmission constraints, through its inaugural Longer-term Transmission Planning procurement — a competitive solicitation rather than traditional planning.
why_it_matters: ISO-NE picked a $2.2bn Avangrid and Eversource project as its preliminary preferred solution to Maine transmission constraints, the first large award under a competitive long-term procurement rather than traditional planning. It validates a model FERC has pushed since Order 1000 that had produced little in practice. Awarding it to incumbent transmission owners will fuel the argument that these solicitations do not really open the market to independents.
why_you_care: Avangrid again, on the regulated side: a $2.2bn preliminary preferred solution is a live New England transmission capex datapoint and the first real output from competitive procurement since Order 1000.

headline: Flexential buys 110 acres in Kaufman County, Texas for a Dallas-area campus scaling to 108MW
players: Flexential, whose investor group includes MSIP alongside GI Partners, GI Data Infrastructure and Hamilton Lane, acquired 110 acres in Talty, Kaufman County, southeast of the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex. Phase one is 36MW across 375,000 sq ft, with a total build-out potential of 108MW across three 36MW buildings. Site work begins early 2027 with customer availability late 2028; investment amount not disclosed.
why_it_matters: Flexential, whose investor group includes MSIP alongside GI Partners, GI Data Infrastructure and Hamilton Lane, bought 110 acres in Talty, Kaufman County southeast of Dallas-Fort Worth. Phase one is 36MW across 375,000 sq ft, with build-out potential of 108MW in three buildings; site work starts early 2027 and customers arrive late 2028. Amount undisclosed, so this is land-banking optionality, not committed capex.
why_you_care: MSIP-backed Flexential land-banking 110 acres for a 108MW Dallas campus, amount undisclosed, so optionality rather than committed capex. A direct read on how the firm is deploying in data centres.

headline: CMA CGM and Stonepeak complete formation of UNITED PORTS LLC; Stonepeak takes 25% for $2.4bn
players: Stonepeak closed its 25% acquisition in UNITED PORTS LLC for $2.4bn, with CMA CGM holding 75% and full operational control, implying roughly $10bn total valuation. The JV holds nine terminals: Fenix Marine Services (Los Angeles), Port Liberty (New York/Bayonne), Santos (Brazil), CSP Valencia, CSP Bilbao and TTI Algeciras (Spain), Kaohsiung (Taiwan), Gemalink (Vietnam), and Nhava Sheva Freeport Terminal (India, pending regulatory approval). Stonepeak may invest up to a further $3.6bn for future opportunities.
why_it_matters: Stonepeak closed its 25% stake in UNITED PORTS LLC for $2.4bn, implying roughly $10bn total, with CMA CGM holding 75% and full operational control. The JV holds nine terminals, including Fenix Marine in Los Angeles and Port Liberty in New York, plus assets in Spain, Brazil, Taiwan, Vietnam and India, where Nhava Sheva is pending approval. CMA CGM's own throughput anchors volumes, and the real option is Stonepeak's up-to-$3.6bn follow-on capacity.
why_you_care: Stonepeak paying $2.4bn for 25% of a nine-terminal ports JV, roughly $10bn implied, is exactly the asset type your LOGISTEC and Termont work covers, with up to $3.6bn more behind it.

headline: A 3-GW data center load loss in Northern Virginia — the largest yet — accelerates mandatory ride-through rules
players: A transmission line fault in Northern Virginia in July 2026 caused roughly 3 GW of data center load to drop off the PJM system, the largest such event to date and double the 1.5 GW lost in a July 2024 Northern Virginia fault. NERC issued a Level 3 alert in May 2026 on data center grid risks and published reliability guidance recommending voluntary ride-through adoption in interconnection studies, with plans to subject data centers to standards similar to power plants; final standards require FERC approval and may be years away. ERCOT ride-through rules were approved and take effect August 1, 2026, requiring new large loads to stay connected during disturbances, with existing data centers required to report non-compliance within 180 days. Companies including ON.Energy and Verrus are developing UPS and microgrid-capable designs for compliance.
why_it_matters: A Northern Virginia line fault dropped roughly 3GW of data centre load off PJM, double the 1.5GW lost in a July 2024 fault. Ride-through is heading toward a hard interconnection requirement, and retrofitting an existing facility's electrical architecture is expensive, a real capex liability inside operating portfolios that most models miss. ERCOT's rules take effect August 1, with existing sites required to report non-compliance within 180 days.
why_you_care: Ride-through retrofits are a real capex liability inside operating data centre portfolios that most models miss; ERCOT's rules take effect August 1, so Texas prices it first.

headline: Blackstone, Brookfield and KKR sign $16bn Kuwait crude pipeline partnership, the country's largest ever FDI
players: Kuwait Oil Company signed a $16bn infrastructure partnership, codenamed Project Peregrine, with a consortium of Blackstone, Brookfield and KKR covering 13 crude oil pipelines spanning roughly 320km of Kuwait's domestic and export network. The consortium takes 49% of the joint venture in equal roughly 16.33% stakes, with KOC retaining 51% and operational control; KOC receives $7.85bn of upfront proceeds at closing. The JV grants KOC exclusive use and operating rights for 20.5 years in exchange for a volume-based tariff; KPC called it the largest foreign direct investment in Kuwait's history.
why_it_matters: In substance a sale-and-leaseback: the sponsors own pipelines they do not operate and collect a volume-based tariff from a state oil company for 20.5 years, so the risk is throughput and convertibility rather than operations. A volume-linked rather than fixed tariff gives growth participation but removes the availability-payment floor infrastructure buyers usually insist on. KOC keeps 51% and control, taking $7.85bn upfront.
why_you_care: Three sponsors splitting 49% equally is how country risk gets spread, on a structure that is really a sale-and-leaseback with a volume tariff and no availability floor.

headline: CenterPoint says 14 GW qualifies under Texas' new SB6 large-load interconnection rules, backed by ~$900M of customer deposits
players: Texas regulators approved new large-load interconnection rules in June 2026 implementing Senate Bill 6, and CenterPoint reported on July 28, 2026 that of 17 GW submitted into the first 'Batch Zero' process, roughly 14 GW should qualify as base load or studied load — a more than 65% increase over its current Houston-area peak of 21 GW. Ten GW have all required ERCOT studies approved and 4 GW have one of two complete; nearly all are expected online by end-2030. The projects are supported by facility extension agreements and approximately $900 million in customer deposits. The PUCT draft rule (16 TAC 25.194) applied to interconnections of 75 MW or more with a $50,000/MW non-refundable fee and $50,000/MW of financial security.
why_it_matters: CenterPoint filed more than 17 GW into ERCOT's new large-load process and expects 14 GW to qualify, backed by signed facility extension agreements and about $900m of customer cash and deposits. Cash collateral is the first credible filter separating real load from phantom load in a US market, which firms up the demand curve behind ERCOT power pricing and favours balance-sheet hyperscalers over thin colocation sponsors.
why_you_care: Cash collateral is the first credible filter separating real load from phantom, so this firms up the demand curve behind ERCOT pricing and favours balance-sheet hyperscalers over thin colocation sponsors.

headline: PJM states seek Section 205 filing rights at FERC as former chairman Kelliher calls the proposal unlawful
players: On July 27, 2026 the Organization of PJM States recommended that PJM and its transmission owners be required to make Federal Power Act Section 205 filings at states' request, arguing PJM's governance and stakeholder process were built for a different era. Former FERC Chairman Joseph Kelliher countered that Section 205 filing rights belong exclusively to public utilities, that states are complainants under Section 206, and that the proposal mirrors a rejected 1984 case, Massachusetts Dept. of Public Utilities v. FERC. The proposal sits in the PJM governance record following Chairman Swett's warning that FERC will impose reforms if PJM does not act by end-September.
why_it_matters: The Organization of PJM States wants PJM and its transmission owners required to make Section 205 filings at states' request. Former FERC chairman Joseph Kelliher calls it unlawful, arguing 205 rights belong to public utilities while states are complainants under 206, and citing a rejected 1984 case. Granted, it would let states bypass PJM's stakeholder process and tilt tariff outcomes toward retail affordability over generator revenue adequacy.
why_you_care: Structural risk to merchant power returns in PJM: state-forced tariff filings would tilt outcomes toward retail affordability over generator revenue adequacy. Contested as unlawful, so watch rather than mark.

headline: Japan's GPIF added nearly $2.5bn to its infrastructure portfolio in FY2025 with only 4% invested domestically
players: Infrastructure Investor reported on July 27, 2026 that Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund added nearly $2.5 billion to its infrastructure portfolio in FY2025 and that only 4% of the portfolio is invested within Japan. GPIF is recruiting a new domestic infrastructure manager. Separately, on July 22, 2026 Infrastructure Investor reported Temasek plans a significant increase in AI-related exposure.
why_it_matters: Infrastructure Investor reported that Japan's GPIF added nearly $2.5bn to its infrastructure portfolio in FY2025 with only 4% of the book invested inside Japan, and is recruiting a domestic infrastructure manager. Separately, Temasek plans a significant increase in AI-related exposure. The world's largest pension staying overwhelmingly ex-Japan keeps the bid under North American and European managers.
why_you_care: Background on LP flows. The world's largest pension staying overwhelmingly ex-Japan keeps the bid under North American and European managers, alongside Temasek's planned AI push. Not actionable.

headline: MSIP to acquire Epic Energy, owner of the Moomba to Adelaide Pipeline System in South Australia
players: MSIP, through funds managed by Morgan Stanley Investment Management, agreed to acquire Epic Energy, the Australian owner-operator of the Moomba to Adelaide Pipeline System (MAPS). Terms undisclosed; close expected in H2 2026 subject to regulatory approvals. Epic's portfolio spans over 1,200km of South Australian gas transmission across MAPS and the South East Pipeline System, plus wind, solar and microgrid assets; MAPS has a 50-year-plus operating history and is one of only two pipeline systems serving Adelaide.
why_it_matters: MSIP agreed to acquire Epic Energy, owner of the Moomba to Adelaide Pipeline System, one of only two pipeline systems serving Adelaide within over 1,200km of South Australian transmission; terms undisclosed, close expected H2 2026. Value comes from tariff resets and recontracting the shipper book more than growth capex. MSIP's language about sourcing through long-standing relationships signals a bilateral or limited process, which usually means a more forgiving entry multiple.
why_you_care: This is the deal to know walking in: bilateral sourcing, mid-market, monopoly-adjacent cash flows, with value from tariff resets and recontracting the shipper book rather than growth capex.

headline: LevelTen Q2 2026: solar PPAs fall 4.8% to $61.40/MWh — first decline in two years — while wind rises to $83.79/MWh
players: LevelTen Energy's Q2 2026 North American PPA Price Index put solar at $61.40/MWh (25th percentile $52.65) and wind at $83.79/MWh (25th percentile $61.19), for a blended average of $72.60/MWh. Solar fell 4.8% quarter over quarter — its first decline in two years — though only 1.8% excluding California, which accounted for more than half the continental decrease. Wind rose 5.5% quarter over quarter and 17.5% year over year, attributed to high fuel and logistics costs and federal permitting friction including Department of Defense delays on national security mitigation agreements since August 2025. LevelTen flagged the July 4, 2026 construction-start deadline under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, after which the pool of tax-credit-eligible US projects effectively freezes.
why_it_matters: The benchmark marks: solar at $61.40/MWh, down 4.8% and its first fall in two years, versus wind at $83.79/MWh, up 17.5% year over year. Contracted valuations for the two technologies are moving in opposite directions. The July 4 construction-start deadline under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act freezes the pool of tax-credit-eligible projects, so expect a two-tier market: safe-harboured pipelines at a premium, everything else clearing on merchant economics.
why_you_care: The PPA marks to value renewables against: solar at $61.40/MWh, down 4.8%, versus wind at $83.79/MWh, up 17.5% year over year, moving in opposite directions.

headline: Brightline Florida wins fifth AAFOH and 14th commuter indenture extension, pushing payments to July 30-31
players: Holders of Brightline Florida's $1.2bn unrated tax-exempt AAFOH bonds and $985m commuter bonds agreed to move the AAFOH debt payment to July 31 and the commuter mandatory redemption to July 30, with commuter interest also due July 31. Bond Buyer reports this is the fifth AAFOH supplement and the 14th commuter indenture supplement. Reported holders include First Eagle, Nuveen, Invesco, BlackRock and Macquarie; Assured Guaranty insures roughly 51% of the $2.2bn senior bonds, and hedge funds hold $1.1bn of subordinate taxable notes against total debt of about $5.5bn.
why_it_matters: Extensions have compressed from months to days, a fifth AAFOH supplement and a fourteenth commuter one, which says no consensual deal is documented and creditors are pricing optionality week by week. Assured Guaranty, insuring roughly 51% of the $2.2bn senior bonds, effectively controls whether this stays out of court. Commuter holders are the most exposed, since their security rests on county payments that are not yet contractually committed.
why_you_care: Extensions compressed from months to days on your Brightline deal, and Assured Guaranty, insuring roughly 51% of the $2.2bn senior bonds, effectively controls whether this stays out of court.

headline: Brookfield named preferred financing partner in $10bn NAVER-NVIDIA Korean AI factory expansion to 200MW
players: NAVER, NVIDIA and Brookfield announced a $10bn package to expand Korea's national AI factory infrastructure. NVIDIA is investing $1bn (1.48 trillion won) for a 4.5% stake via 7,241,564 new shares at 204,500 won, becoming NAVER's third-largest shareholder, with payment due 30 October. Brookfield was selected as exclusive preferred negotiating partner to arrange the remaining roughly $9bn of computing infrastructure funding, likely through project finance, on a non-binding term sheet; capacity scales from 55MW in H1 2027 to 100MW by end-2027 and 200MW in 2028, with a long-term 1GW target.
why_it_matters: Brookfield was named exclusive preferred negotiating partner, on a non-binding term sheet, to arrange roughly $9bn of the $10bn NAVER AI factory expansion. That is the arranger seat rather than the equity seat, which fits a single national-champion offtaker and a three-year refresh cycle. NVIDIA's $1bn for 4.5% is conditional on the financing, so Brookfield's mandate gates the deal; capacity scales from 55MW to 200MW by 2028.
why_you_care: Brookfield took the arranger seat, not the equity seat, on roughly $9bn of Korean AI factory financing on a non-binding term sheet, a signal that sovereign AI is its own asset class.

headline: PJM board proposes 15-year backstop capacity auction at a $555/MW-day cap plus an interim data center curtailment service
players: PJM's board on July 27, 2026 directed two FERC filings: a reliability backstop procurement to close the 6.8 GW shortfall, running September 30 to October 21, 2026 for 15-year commitments at a $555/MW-day cap with resources required online by June 1, 2032; and an Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) allowing curtailment of new large loads lacking their own supply during grid emergencies. A bilateral matchmaking process overseen by Charles River Associates was expected to produce initial matches in August, and PJM will create a large load registry tracking facility details and capacity supply.
why_it_matters: PJM's board directed two FERC filings: a reliability backstop procurement to close the 6.8 GW shortfall, running September 30 to October 21, 2026, with 15-year commitments at a $555/MW-day cap and resources online by June 1, 2032; and an interim service (IRAS) allowing curtailment of new large loads lacking their own supply. Fifteen years at $555 is the most bankable revenue PJM has offered, splitting the market in two.
why_you_care: The most bankable revenue PJM has offered, 15 years at a $555/MW-day cap for new gas, storage and uprates, while IRAS quietly weakens the firmness of large-load offtake.

headline: KKR and ECP agree £5.75bn take-private of DCC Energy at 6,525p per share
players: KKR and Energy Capital Partners, through Dragon Bidco, agreed to acquire DCC Energy for £5.75bn via a court-sanctioned scheme of arrangement at 6,525p per share in cash plus a 147.22p final dividend, a 24% premium to the 5,380p undisturbed price. Shareholders may receive up to a further 125p per share if the Nexora technology business is sold by 31 July 2027. An initial April bid at 5,800p was rejected before the consortium raised to 6,525p in June; the board unanimously recommended the improved terms and completion is expected in Q1 2027.
why_it_matters: KKR and ECP agreed to take DCC Energy private for GBP5.75bn at 6,525p a share plus a 147.22p final dividend, a 24% premium to the 5,380p undisturbed price, with up to 125p more if Nexora is sold by 31 July 2027; an April bid at 5,800p was rejected. DCC distributes LPG and liquid fuels on unit margins, so returns must come from bolt-ons and margin, not re-rating. Completion expected Q1 2027.
why_you_care: Two-stage bid mechanics at a 24% premium with contingent consideration on a non-core asset. On unit-margin fuel distribution, returns have to come from bolt-ons and margin, not re-rating.

headline: Panama Canal cuts draft to 49 feet on El Nino risk even as transit revenue rises 17% to $4.8bn
players: The Panama Canal Authority reduced maximum draft for neo-Panamax vessels to 49 feet effective July 24, 2026, with a further reduction scheduled for August 15 if dry conditions persist. Administrator Ricaurte Vasquez warned capacity restrictions could extend to reductions in daily booking slots. For October 2025 through June 2026 the canal averaged 35 daily transits and handled 10,726 vessels, up 5.2% year on year, moving 390 million PC/UMS tons (up 7%), generating $4.8 billion of transit revenue (up 17%) and $3.6 billion of net income (up 19%). MSC, Hapag-Lloyd and CMA CGM announced canal surcharges of $100, $130 and $320 per TEU respectively.
why_it_matters: Revenue up 17% on volume up 5% is the canal monetising scarcity through price, which is the model for any capacity-constrained transport concession. But the draft cut to 49 feet confirms hydrology, not demand, is the binding constraint, and it is recurring rather than a one-off. Carriers passed through surcharges of $100 to $320 per TEU, so shippers absorb the cost.
why_you_care: Scarcity priced through toll rather than volume, revenue up 17% on transits up 5%, the model for any capacity-constrained transport concession and a routing risk for gateway throughput.

headline: PG&E reports a 12.7-GW data center pipeline but only 490 MW with executed interconnection agreements
players: PG&E reported a 12.7 GW data center pipeline on July 24, 2026, of which only 490 MW has executed interconnection agreements and 3.9 GW is in final engineering. The utility expects to serve 1.8 GW of new data center load by 2030. The pipeline swung from 7.3 GW at end-2025 down to 5.4 GW in Q1 2026 before rebounding, reflecting stricter project vetting; smaller data centers under 1 GW make up the bulk of the current queue. CEO Patti Poppe said the aim is pricing 'attractive to data center customers, but still rate-reducing for our other customers.'
why_it_matters: PG&E shows a 12.7 GW data center pipeline but only 490 MW with executed interconnection agreements, around 4%, and expects to serve 1.8 GW by 2030. That gap is the cleanest available measure of announced versus real conversion and argues for heavily discounting the load-growth narratives embedded in utility valuations and data center land pricing. Executed-IA megawatts is the disclosure that actually matters.
why_you_care: Your default haircut on any data centre pipeline: 12.7 GW announced against 490 MW with executed interconnection agreements, and 1.8 GW expected to be served by 2030.

headline: FERC Chairman Swett tells PJM to adopt governance reforms by end of September or FERC will impose them
players: FERC Chairman Laura Swett said on July 24, 2026 that PJM faces 'a grave legitimacy crisis' and that market participants 'have lost confidence in PJM's decision-making abilities,' warning FERC will impose governance reforms if PJM does not adopt them by the end of September. Reform concepts on the table include greater board independence, a formal state role, Section 205 filing rights for states, expanded PJM filing rights, a shift to an advisory stakeholder process on the MISO model, and codifying public interest in PJM's mission. FERC will convene a dispute resolution forum with PJM stakeholders in September.
why_it_matters: Governance controls the tariff, and the tariff sets the revenue stack for every generator and storage asset in the largest US power market. Swett calling it 'a grave legitimacy crisis' and threatening to impose reforms by end-September raises the odds that state filing rights or an advisory stakeholder model shift rulemaking toward retail affordability politics, a negative for merchant power in PJM. Real process risk for any PJM asset.
why_you_care: Process risk on anything you value in PJM. Governance sets the tariff, and a shift toward state filing rights or an advisory stakeholder model would cut against merchant power.

headline: FERC launches a grid-enhancing technologies task force and signals incentive-based support for advanced transmission
players: FERC Chairman Laura Swett said on July 23, 2026 that the agency has created a task force on grid-enhancing technologies to examine how it can support them, possibly with incentives. Because the Federal Power Act bars technology mandates, FERC intends to direct transmission owners to analyse GETs in planning, fold GET consideration into transmission incentive programmes, and require incentive applicants to justify technology choices. Commissioner Judy Chang said companies could be required to explain what they are implementing and why they are not using the best available technologies, and that FERC should find efficiencies through competition 15 years after Order 1000. No rulemaking timeline was announced.
why_it_matters: FERC Chairman Laura Swett said the agency has created a task force on grid-enhancing technologies, potentially with incentives. The Federal Power Act bars technology mandates, so FERC would instead make transmission owners analyse GETs in planning and justify technology choices in incentive applications. Dynamic line ratings, power flow controllers and high-performance conductors unlock existing capacity far cheaper and faster than new lines. No rulemaking timeline was announced.
why_you_care: One to monitor, not act on. Incentive treatment would rate-base grid-enhancing technologies and modestly shrink greenfield transmission capex; no rulemaking timeline was announced.

headline: STB orders UP and NS to make merger employee-impact exhibits public after union objections
players: The Surface Transportation Board ordered Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to redesignate as public the exhibits detailing merger employment effects — positions to be abolished, created or transferred — after rail labor argued the carriers had improperly marked them highly confidential. The Board found the information had been publicly disclosed in prior merger proceedings and did not appear commercially sensitive. The carriers were required to refile the public versions by July 27, 2026.
why_it_matters: Putting the job-loss exhibits on the public record as the evidentiary phase opens raises the political and legislative risk around approval, and makes the merger's crew and craft consolidation synergies testable by unions and state officials. New York Dock labor protective conditions are the most likely place the Board adds cost. For rail-adjacent services such as car repair, terminal switching and transload, the exhibits map where volumes and headcount are expected to move.
why_you_care: Rail-adjacent background: the synergy case is now public, which is usually where merger economics get renegotiated, and the exhibits map where volumes and headcount are expected to move.

headline: Meridiam refinances Netcity Telecom with EUR80m, Romania's first project finance bond at 26.5-year tenor
players: Meridiam completed an EUR 80 million refinancing of Netcity Telecom, Bucharest's underground telecommunications network, with tenor of up to 26.5 years described as a new market record and the first project finance bond issuance in Romania. Lenders comprised an international institutional investor, an international bank and a local Romanian bank. Netcity operates over 3,000km of underground telecoms infrastructure serving approximately 70,000 buildings and nearly 600,000 homes and offices under a 49-year municipal concession running since 2008. Meridiam holds 80% and E-INFRA Group 20%.
why_it_matters: Meridiam refinanced Netcity Telecom, Bucharest's underground telecoms network, with EUR80m at up to 26.5 years, described as Romania's first project finance bond. Netcity runs over 3,000km of duct serving nearly 600,000 homes and offices under a 49-year municipal concession dating to 2008, exactly the monopoly profile that supports very long amortising debt. The bigger win is a Romanian project bond benchmark others can reuse across CEE.
why_you_care: A 26.5-year tenor against a 49-year municipal concession is a useful long-dated financing precedent; otherwise CEE digital infrastructure colour, not actionable.

headline: Drewry World Container Index falls 4% to $4,374 per FEU on capacity growth and softer demand
players: The Drewry World Container Index fell 4% to $4,374 per 40-foot container in the week to July 23, 2026, a second consecutive weekly decline. Shanghai-Los Angeles fell 6% to $5,878, Shanghai-New York fell 4% to $7,598, Shanghai-Genoa fell 5% to $5,988 and Shanghai-Rotterdam fell 1% to $4,824. Drivers were additional vessel capacity and softer demand, with blank sailings decreasing. Carriers announced Emergency Fuel Surcharges for August related to Strait of Hormuz tensions, which had not yet reversed the declines.
why_it_matters: Drewry's World Container Index fell 4% to $4,374 per FEU in the week to July 23, a second consecutive decline, with Shanghai-Los Angeles down 6% to $5,878, Shanghai-New York down 4% to $7,598 and Shanghai-Rotterdam down 1% to $4,824. Added vessel capacity and softer demand are the drivers, with fewer blank sailings. August emergency fuel surcharges tied to Strait of Hormuz tensions have not reversed it.
why_you_care: Freight rates are not terminal revenue, but thin carrier margins shape stevedoring tariff talks. Useful colour around LOGISTEC/Termont rather than something to act on.

headline: Line fault drops roughly 3 GW of data center load in Virginia, sharpening the case for load ride-through standards
players: RTO Insider reported on July 23, 2026 that a transmission line fault caused approximately 3 GW of data center load to disconnect in Virginia. The event follows FERC's July 16 directive to NERC to develop reliability standards for computational large loads by the end of 2026.
why_it_matters: Losing roughly 3 GW of load at once is the mirror image of a generator trip and destabilises voltage and frequency over a wide area, which is why FERC has directed NERC to write mandatory large-load standards by the end of 2026. Expect retrofit obligations and possible operating restrictions for data centres in dense corridors, and more value for fast-responding resources and reactive power.
why_you_care: Mandatory large-load ride-through standards due by the end of 2026 add a retrofit cost line to data centre underwriting and lift the value of fast-responding generation and reactive power.

headline: Partners Group wraps debut infrastructure secondaries effort at $5.5bn, seven times its original target
players: Partners Group closed its debut infrastructure secondaries effort with $5.5bn raised in total, comprising $1.7bn in the Partners Group Infrastructure Secondary fund vehicle and $3.8bn in bespoke separate mandates. The original target was $750m. LP composition was not disclosed.
why_it_matters: The split is the story: $3.8bn of bespoke mandates against a $1.7bn commingled fund raised on a $750m target. Large LPs want infrastructure secondaries exposure on their own terms and fee schedules, not through a blind pool. Raising more than seven times target confirms demand far exceeds deal supply, a mismatch that pushes pricing toward par and erodes the discount the strategy depends on.
why_you_care: Infrastructure secondaries raised more than seven times target, with $3.8bn of it in bespoke mandates: demand outrunning deal supply, which pushes pricing toward par. Background market colour.

headline: Meridiam leads EUR23m investment in Chargepoly for heavy-duty EV fleet charging infrastructure
players: Meridiam, through its Green Impact Growth Fund, led a EUR 23 million investment in Chargepoly alongside Fideve Groupe. Founded in 2019 and headquartered in Aix-en-Provence, Chargepoly designs and operates DC charging infrastructure for heavy-duty vehicle fleets across France, the UK and Canada, combining modular charging hardware with power-allocation software called Lucie, tested across 50+ heavy-duty vehicle models. Proceeds fund international expansion and platform development. Customers include CMA-CGM, with OEM partnerships including Renault Trucks, Volvo and Daimler.
why_it_matters: Meridiam led a EUR 23m investment in Chargepoly, which builds and operates DC charging for heavy-duty fleets across France, the UK and Canada. Depot charging beats public charging because utilisation is contracted against a known fleet, and Chargepoly's Lucie software shares one constrained grid connection across many charge points, avoiding the substation upgrades that kill most heavy-duty electrification cases. This is growth equity, not infrastructure yield.
why_you_care: Growth equity, not infrastructure yield, but the framing travels: the constrained grid connection shared across many charge points is the scarce asset, not the hardware.

headline: CSX posts record $3.94bn quarterly revenue with 38.3% operating margin and 9% intermodal volume growth
players: CSX reported second quarter 2026 revenue of $3.94 billion on July 22, 2026, up 10% year on year and a record, with diluted EPS of $0.54 up 23%, operating income of $1.51 billion up 17% and operating margin of 38.3%, an expansion of 240 basis points. Total volume rose 6% to 1.68 million units, led by 9% intermodal growth with broad-based gains in merchandise and coal. Growth was driven by higher fuel surcharge revenue plus volume and pricing across merchandise, intermodal and coal.
why_it_matters: A 240 basis point margin expansion on 6% volume growth shows incremental margins on Eastern rail are still very high, the core argument for rail as infrastructure rather than a cyclical industrial. But a meaningful share of the revenue gain is fuel surcharge, pass-through that reverses when diesel falls, so strip it out before capitalising growth. Intermodal up 9% while NS is under merger review suggests competitive dynamics are already shifting.
why_you_care: Rail benchmark for FTAI Infrastructure's railroad segment: 240 basis points of margin expansion on 6% volume, but strip the fuel surcharge before capitalising that growth.

headline: Bloom Energy survey: 61% of data center developers would turn to onsite power, and a third of US data centers seen fully off-grid by 2030
players: Bloom Energy's mid-year 2026 data center power report, based on 156 respondents surveyed in Q2 2026 including hyperscalers, colocation providers, neoclouds, developers and chip developers (79% US-based), found power availability cited as a top-three site selection factor by 51%, down from 84% in June 2025 but still dominant. When grid power becomes a constraint, 61% would deploy onsite power as their primary strategy, and industry leaders expect roughly one-third of US data centers to run entirely on onsite power by 2030. On community risk, 28% of developers said local opposition worsened over the past six months, over 70% of Americans oppose AI data centers near their homes, and communities have blocked or delayed more than $64 billion in projects. Other worsening barriers: construction costs 35%, grid upgrade costs 28%, critical equipment availability 26%. Only 33% had invested in grid support and resiliency and 29% in minimizing water consumption.
why_it_matters: Bloom's mid-year survey of 156 data center players found 61% would make onsite power their primary answer to grid constraints, with leaders expecting about a third of US data centers fully off-grid by 2030. That moves generation out of utility rate base into privately owned contracted assets funds can buy. Community opposition has blocked or delayed over $64bn of projects, yet only 33% have invested in grid support.
why_you_care: Onsite power moving from utility rate base into privately owned contracted assets is the buy-side opening here, and $64bn of community-blocked projects makes social licence a costable underwriting input.

headline: We Energies seeks to acquire two Invenergy gas plants totaling 1,510 MW for $2.26B to serve Microsoft and Vantage data centers
players: Two Invenergy-developed gas plants in southeastern Wisconsin are under regulatory review: the 1,186-MW Red Oak Ridge Energy Center and the 324-MW Foundry Ridge Energy Center, together representing a $2.26 billion investment, which We Energies plans to acquire if approved. The plants are designed to serve hyperscale demand from a Microsoft campus and a Vantage project leased to OpenAI and Oracle. Data centers are projected to represent 68% of Wisconsin's electricity demand growth by 2030. The dispute centers on Wisconsin's two-step review, in which construction approval precedes the utility acquisition review, so by the time a utility must demonstrate public need the plant is already set for construction.
why_it_matters: IPP builds, then utility buys, is becoming the dominant route to new gas capacity, and it favours sponsors: development risk is taken privately and monetised onto a regulated balance sheet at close. Wisconsin's two-step review, where construction approval precedes the acquisition review, effectively pre-commits the regulator and improves exit certainty. The risk is states inserting a needs test before construction.
why_you_care: The monetisation route for gas development platforms: build privately, sell onto a regulated balance sheet, with Wisconsin's two-step review pre-committing the regulator. $2.26bn for 1,510 MW.

headline: GE Vernova gas turbine backlog hits 116 GW with 63 GW of slot reservations; 2031 slots now being sold
players: GE Vernova reported Q2 2026 gas turbine backlog of 116 GW, up from 100 GW in Q1 and targeting 125 GW by year-end, split between 53 GW of equipment backlog and 63 GW of slot reservations. Power segment orders were $16.7 billion, up 134% organically; the company shipped 3 GW, signed 20 GW of orders and slot reservations, and converted 10 GW of reservations to firm orders. Management said it is taking reservations for 2031 deliveries and expects to be more than halfway contracted for 2031 by year-end; third-party analyst estimates cited pricing of roughly $790/kW for heavy-duty turbines, $950/kW for HA-class combined cycle and $1,800/kW for aeroderivatives. Data center orders exceeded $5 billion year to date, more than double all of 2025, and capacity is targeted to grow from 20 GW annualized to 30 GW by 2030.
why_it_matters: Turbine slots, not capital or land, are the binding constraint on new dispatchable capacity: backlog is 116GW, GE Vernova is selling 2031 delivery slots and expects to be more than half contracted for 2031 by year-end. That makes an existing slot or an already-permitted gas project a tradeable asset. Analyst-estimated pricing of about $790/kW heavy-duty, $950/kW HA-class combined cycle and $1,800/kW aeroderivative gives you hard inputs for greenfield gas.
why_you_care: Hard greenfield gas inputs at roughly $790/kW heavy-duty, $950/kW HA-class combined cycle and $1,800/kW aeroderivative, with a 2031 turbine slot now itself the scarce asset.

headline: Brookfield to buy battery storage platform Aypa Power from Blackstone at about $7bn enterprise value
players: Brookfield Asset Management, through its second flagship global transition fund, agreed to acquire Aypa Power from Blackstone Energy Transition Partners at an enterprise value of roughly $7bn and equity value of about $3bn. Aypa has 6.5GW operating, under construction or contracted and a development pipeline of more than 20GW across 70-plus projects; the operating and under-construction portfolio is 95% contracted with investment-grade offtakers on an average remaining contract duration of 17 years. Blackstone acquired the predecessor business, NRStor C&I, in 2020 with 0.2GWh of capacity and rebranded it to Aypa while pivoting to utility scale, a roughly six-year hold.
why_it_matters: Brookfield agreed to buy Aypa Power from Blackstone at roughly $7bn enterprise value and about $3bn equity. A fleet that is 95% contracted with investment-grade offtakers on a 17-year average remaining tenor is a genuinely core cash-flow profile, which is why it clears at an infrastructure multiple. Blackstone took a 0.2GWh C&I business to 6.5GW plus a 20GW-plus pipeline in about six years.
why_you_care: The reference price for independent storage platforms at roughly $7bn enterprise value. Use it when you mark Hydrostor's pipeline or build a storage comp set.

headline: Brookfield Infrastructure to collapse BIP and BIPC into a single corporation to widen index eligibility
players: Brookfield Infrastructure announced plans to merge BIP, its limited partnership, and BIPC, its corporate vehicle, into a single listed corporation, BIP Inc, on a one-for-one exchange for both unitholders and exchangeable shareholders. Management cited broadening the investor base, supporting index demand and removing partnership tax reporting. Special meetings are set for 14 October 2026 with a 21 August 2026 record date and completion expected in Q4 2026; the transaction is expected to be tax-deferred for Canadian and US investors.
why_it_matters: Brookfield plans to collapse BIP and BIPC into one corporation, BIP Inc, one-for-one. The dual structure traded at a discount because index funds and many US taxable investors avoid K-1 partnerships, so this is valuation arbitrage rather than anything operational: index inclusion mechanically adds passive demand for the same cash flows. Special meetings are set for 14 October with completion expected in Q4 2026.
why_you_care: Listed-comp housekeeping: a one-for-one collapse chasing index demand, relevant only if BIP sits in your trading comps set or you are sizing Brookfield's acquisition currency.

headline: Secondary market volume tops $120bn in H1 2026, up 20%, with single-asset continuation vehicles at $34bn
players: PitchBook reported on July 21, 2026 that total secondary deal volume surpassed $120 billion in the first six months of 2026, a 20% increase over H1 2025. GP-led transactions made up 53.7% of overall volume, and single-asset continuation vehicles accounted for $34 billion, more than half of GP-led volume. Secondary buyers' dry powder fell 10% from the start of the year, pushing the capital overhang multiple toward 1.0x.
why_it_matters: Secondary volume topped $120bn in H1 2026, up 20%, with GP-leds at 53.7% and single-asset continuation vehicles at $34bn. Buyer dry powder fell 10%, pushing the capital overhang toward 1.0x, the point where pricing power flips from sellers to buyers. For infra GPs planning continuation vehicles on trophy assets, the window for easy execution at tight discounts is narrowing.
why_you_care: Exit-route colour. With buyer dry powder down 10% and the overhang near 1.0x, pricing power is flipping to buyers, narrowing the window for continuation vehicles on trophy infra assets.

headline: BNEF nearly doubles its US data center power forecast to 194 GW by 2035; chip-based model implies 207 GW by 2033
players: BloombergNEF raised its US data center capacity forecast to 194 GW by 2035, 83% above its December 2025 outlook, and to 118 GW by 2030, a 52% increase, equating to roughly 20% of US electricity consumption. A second BNEF model built around expected AI chip deliveries implies 207 GW by 2033, a 63 GW gap to the base case. BNEF noted it underestimated 2025 capacity by 16% and that more than 70 projects in the pipeline are now 1 GW or larger. Head of technology and innovation Mark Daly cautioned the forecast 'could be too generous' given competition for labor and power equipment and widespread local opposition. For context, S&P Global expects 180 GW by 2030 and Bank of America projects data centers adding roughly 125 GW of load.
why_it_matters: BNEF lifted its US data centre forecast to 194 GW by 2035, 83% above its December 2025 outlook, and 118 GW by 2030, about 20% of US electricity. A separate model built on AI chip deliveries implies 207 GW by 2033. BNEF admits it undershot 2025 capacity by 16%, has 70-plus gigawatt-scale projects in its pipeline, and warns the number could be too generous. S&P sees 180 GW by 2030.
why_you_care: The demand number underpinning every power and data centre underwrite, now 194 GW by 2035, with BNEF's own caveat that the forecast could be too generous.

headline: Macquarie completes $40bn exit of Aligned Data Centers to AIP, MGX and GIP consortium after eight-year hold
players: Macquarie Asset Management completed the sale of Aligned Data Centers to a consortium comprising the AI Infrastructure Partnership, MGX and BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners. The transaction was announced in October 2025 at a US$40bn enterprise value. Under Macquarie's eight-year ownership from 2018, Aligned grew from two facilities with 85MW to 51 campuses and more than 6.4GW of operational and planned capacity across the Americas; returns to MAM were not disclosed.
why_it_matters: Macquarie completed the sale of Aligned Data Centers to a consortium of the AI Infrastructure Partnership, MGX and BlackRock's GIP, at the $40bn enterprise value announced in October 2025, roughly $6.25m per MW of operational and planned capacity. Over eight years Macquarie took Aligned from two facilities and 85MW to 51 campuses and more than 6.4GW. Returns to MAM undisclosed.
why_you_care: The benchmark every hyperscale platform now gets marked against: $40bn enterprise value, roughly $6.25m per MW, and 85MW to 6.4GW over an eight-year hold.

headline: Alberta regulator approves ATCO's 146-mile, C$2.9bn Yellowhead gas pipeline at over 1.1 Bcf/d
players: The Alberta Utilities Commission granted final approval for ATCO's Yellowhead Mainline, a 235-kilometre (146-mile), 36-inch natural gas transmission pipeline running from the Peers area to Fort Saskatchewan with one compressor station. Capacity exceeds 1.1 Bcf/d at a capital cost of $2.9 billion. Construction begins immediately, with roughly 2,000 direct construction jobs and an additional 12,000 downstream construction jobs from related industrial developments.
why_it_matters: The Alberta Utilities Commission gave final approval to ATCO's Yellowhead Mainline, 235km (146 miles) of 36-inch gas transmission from Peers to Fort Saskatchewan at over 1.1 Bcf/d for $2.9bn, with construction starting immediately. Because it is rate-regulated rather than merchant, approval effectively locks a $2.9bn rate base addition earning a regulated return. It also relieves gas supply into Alberta's petrochemical and emerging data centre corridor.
why_you_care: Regulated-versus-merchant framing in gas. Final AUC approval locks a $2.9bn rate base addition earning a regulated return, and relieves supply into Alberta's petrochemical and emerging data centre corridor.

headline: PJM market monitor: data centers drove $6.3B of the $16.4B latest capacity auction cost, and $29.4B over four auctions
players: Monitoring Analytics, PJM's independent market monitor, reported that data centers drove $6.3 billion of the $16.4 billion in charges from the most recent capacity auction (38%), and $29.4 billion of $63.6 billion across the last four auctions (46%). President Joseph Bowring argued data centers should either secure their own generation contracts or be served through dedicated 15-year capacity auctions, saying PJM 'is continuing to act like it's business as usual' and that failing to separate large loads 'imposes costs on other customers.'
why_it_matters: PJM's monitor puts data centers at $6.3bn of the $16.4bn latest capacity auction charge and $29.4bn of $63.6bn across four auctions, 46%. Bowring wants them to contract their own generation or be served through dedicated 15-year capacity auctions. Quantifying the cost shift gives regulators the evidence for separate large-load rate structures, and dedicated auctions would create a long-dated capacity revenue stream you could finance new build against.
why_you_care: The number regulators will quote: 46% of four auctions' capacity charges. Dedicated 15-year large-load auctions would create a long-dated revenue stream you could finance new build against.

headline: MISO to build a dedicated expedited study process and non-firm transmission service for large loads
players: RTO Insider reported on July 20, 2026 that MISO will create a new expedited study process for large loads conducted outside its regular interconnection queue, together with a non-firm transmission service option for large loads, as its existing queue fast lane winds down. The design responds to FERC's show cause proceeding in Docket EL26-70.
why_it_matters: MISO is the second RTO after SPP to build a curtailable fast-track for large loads, confirming that non-firm service is becoming the standard bridge product for getting data centres connected. That speeds time-to-power across the Midwest and Delta, which have land, water and gas advantages but slower queues than ERCOT. Because non-firm service is not bankable on its own, it also creates demand for co-located firming generation and storage.
why_you_care: Non-firm service is becoming the standard bridge for connecting data centres, and because it is not bankable alone it creates demand for co-located firming generation and storage.

headline: Enbridge begins construction on C$4bn Sunrise expansion adding 300 MMcf/d on the Westcoast system
players: Enbridge started construction in July 2026 on the $4 billion Sunrise expansion of its Westcoast system in British Columbia, following federal approval in April 2026. The project adds 300 million cubic feet per day via roughly 87 miles (140 km) of new pipeline across 11 looping segments plus compression and facility upgrades, serving BC, Alberta and the US Pacific Northwest. It supports West Coast LNG exports including Woodfibre LNG, and is expected to create about 2,500 construction jobs. Thirty-eight Indigenous communities hold a 12.5% ownership interest in the Westcoast system through a federal loan guarantee programme.
why_it_matters: At roughly $13m per MMcf/d of new capacity, $4bn for 300 MMcf/d is expensive pipe, a measure of how binding BC permitting and terrain are and why existing Western Canadian takeaway should carry a scarcity premium. Sanctioning at this size confirms West Coast LNG is pulling real capital. The 12.5% Indigenous equity stake, backed by a federal loan guarantee, is now standard on Canadian linear infrastructure.
why_you_care: A Canadian midstream capex mark at roughly $13m per MMcf/d, and the 12.5% Indigenous equity stake behind a federal loan guarantee is now standard structure on comparable projects.

headline: Port Houston lines up next wave of terminal and channel spending including $84.6m Barbours Cut wharf rebuild
players: Port Houston is advancing more than $89 million of terminal and channel work: an $84.6 million Russell Marine contract to reconstruct Wharves 5 and 6 at Barbours Cut Container Terminal covering about 1,333 feet of wharf for post-panamax vessels and larger ship-to-shore cranes; a $3.2 million Freese and Nichols contract for environmental planning and permitting on the proposed Barbours Cut Northside Expansion onto Spilman Island with two berthing slips; a $1.5 million cost-share with the US Army Corps of Engineers to begin the Project 12 navigation feasibility study; and $500,000 of continued support on the Project 11 channel widening and deepening programme running through 2030. The port has outlined roughly $650 million of planned Barbours Cut investment between 2023 and 2027.
why_it_matters: Port Houston is advancing more than $89m of work: $84.6m to Russell Marine to rebuild Wharves 5 and 6 at Barbours Cut, about 1,333 feet for post-panamax vessels and larger cranes; $3.2m to Freese and Nichols for permitting on the Spilman Island Northside expansion; $1.5m toward the Project 12 feasibility study; and $500,000 on Project 11.
